header.subtitle: Support the imaging team safely: radiography workflow and image quality, ALARA radiation safety, positioning and restraint support, ultrasound prep, CT/MRI and contrast readiness, and emergency imaging prioritization.
header.askPrompt: What is the Hannah support-staff scope for radiography, ultrasound, CT and MRI, and when should I pause an imaging study and escalate?
header.resourcesBody: Hospital radiation safety policy, dosimetry and PPE rules, positioning aids inventory, ultrasound prep instructions, and the CT/MRI and contrast readiness checklists used in this lesson.
header.resourcesNote: This lesson teaches support tasks only — prepare, monitor, communicate, escalate. It does not teach image interpretation, technique selection, contrast administration, or scanner operation, and it does not replace your hospital's radiation safety policy or local regulations.

overview.heading: Make the right image possible — safely, once, and inside your scope
overview.intro: Diagnostic imaging is a team procedure. Veterinarians and RVTs choose the study and read the images; support staff make it possible — the confirmed order, the calm patient, the correct marker, the shielded room, the staged supplies, and the voice that says “stop, this patient has changed”. This lesson keeps you firmly on the support side of that line: prepare, monitor, communicate, escalate.
objectives: Confirm the imaging order, patient identity, body region, laterality, urgency and safety constraints before the patient moves.
Set up a radiography room using ALARA: minimize time, maximize distance, use shielding, and keep every body part out of the primary beam.
Explain how motion, poor positioning, missing markers and wrong laterality cause retakes and delay care.
Choose low-stress positioning and restraint support, and know when to pause and escalate for sedation, analgesia, oxygen, or reassessment.
Prepare a patient and workspace for abdominal or focused emergency ultrasound without claiming any diagnostic interpretation.
Run CT/MRI support checklists including metal screening, anesthesia and monitoring readiness, transport, and contrast readiness.
Apply the emergency rule: stabilize first, use focused bedside imaging when it changes immediate care, and defer stressful radiographs until the patient can tolerate them.
overview.connectsForward: Imaging Support builds on Sample Collection — the same habits of confirming identity, protecting the sample or study, and escalating early. It feeds forward into anesthesia and monitoring support, emergency and critical care workflows, and every conversation where you describe what you observed rather than what you think it means.

modules.title: Radiography Workflow & Image Quality
modules.completionHeading: Work through the setup audit, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
Radiography is the imaging study you will support most often. Nothing in this module asks you to read a radiograph — it asks you to make the study happen safely, correctly labeled, and right the first time.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

In this module you will

  • Confirm the imaging order, patient identity, body region, laterality, and urgency before the patient moves.
  • Stage markers, positioning aids, PPE, and a restraint plan so the exposure is calm and quick.
  • Explain why motion, wrong or missing markers, and incomplete views cause retakes.
  • Hand the study off with documentation the veterinary team can trust.

Why it matters

Retakes cost the patient, not just the schedule

Radiography is one of the most common diagnostic tools in veterinary practice, and exposure depends on settings such as kVp, mA, and exposure time (Merck Veterinary Manual — Radiography of Animals). A higher mA with a proportionally shorter exposure time can reduce motion blur — but changing technique is the radiographer’s or veterinarian’s call, not yours. Your lever is the setup: a calm patient, a stable position, and one clean exposure.

Cornell’s imaging service puts the practical reason for sedation plainly — animals may need sedation or anesthesia when movement would defeat the study (Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Imaging Service). Recognizing that early, and saying so, is a support skill.

The five-point setup

What you confirm before the patient enters the room

1. Order and region

Read the order yourself. Which study, which body region, how many views, and how urgent?

2. Patient identity

Name, ID, species, and signalment against the order and the room board. Two identifiers, every time.

3. Laterality

Left or right, and which limb. If the order and the whiteboard disagree, stop and ask — never guess.

4. Setup and PPE

Markers within reach, positioning aids staged, gowns, gloves and thyroid shields on the people who need them.

5. Patient plan

Who restrains, who monitors, is sedation planned, and what is the pause signal if the patient deteriorates?

6. After the exposure

Correct patient record, correct study and side, note anything that limited the images, and return the patient to care.

Motion is the enemy you can actually control

Panting, trembling, struggling, and repositioning all blur images. Before anyone reaches for a technique change, ask whether the patient is comfortable, supported, warm, and calm — and whether the plan needs a conversation with the veterinarian or RVT about sedation.

Boundary: you can report “the patient will not hold still and is panting hard”. You do not adjust technique factors or decide on sedation yourself.

Practice

Ready or Not?

Six setups are waiting outside the x-ray room. For each one, decide whether the team can proceed as described or whether something has to be fixed first. One card at a time.

Ready or Not?

Audit each setup before the exposure

Choose Ready to proceed or Fix before exposure. Feedback appears immediately.

  1. Setup 1 of 6

    Lateral thorax on a stable Labrador. Order, patient ID and region are confirmed; positioning aids are staged; PPE is on; but no left or right marker is in the room.

  2. Setup 2 of 6

    The order reads left stifle. The room whiteboard says right stifle. The patient is calm and everything else is staged.

  3. Setup 3 of 6

    A newly admitted dog is panting hard, wriggling, and repeatedly standing up on the table. The team is ready to expose.

  4. Setup 4 of 6

    Order, ID, region, laterality and markers are all confirmed. Positioning aids are staged, the restrainer and monitor are named, hands-free positioning is planned, and PPE is on everyone remaining in the room.

  5. Setup 5 of 6

    No one has said who is staying in the room, and there is no plan for gowns, gloves, or thyroid shields.

  6. Setup 6 of 6

    A dog has been sedated for an abdominal series. Positioning aids are ready and PPE is sorted, but no one has been assigned to watch the patient’s breathing and recovery.

Support staff protect image usability and patient safety. Anything unclear is a question, not a guess.

  • Merck Veterinary Manual — Radiography of Animals
  • Merck Veterinary Manual — Overview of Diagnostic Imaging
  • Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Imaging Service

modules.title: Radiation Safety & ALARA
modules.completionHeading: Complete the ALARA room sweep and the three safety decisions, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
Radiation safety is the highest-risk topic in this lesson. ALARA — as low as reasonably achievable — is not a poster on the wall; it is a set of habits you use every time the beam is on.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

In this module you will

  • State the three basic protective measures — time, distance, and shielding — and use them in a real room.
  • Recognize that no part of any person belongs in the primary beam.
  • Follow local rules for dosimetry, PPE, occupancy, and who may assist.
  • Escalate confidently when a colleague suggests an unsafe shortcut.

The rule

ALARA in three moves

The CDC defines ALARA as “as low as reasonably achievable” and names time, distance, and shielding as the three basic protective measures (CDC — ALARA: As Low As Reasonably Achievable). The American College of Veterinary Radiology states that exposure in veterinary settings should always be kept as low as reasonably achievable while maintaining the quality of the procedure, and that a human body part in the primary beam is a failure of safety protocol (American College of Veterinary Radiology — Radiation Safety Statement).

Time

Fewer exposures, shorter exposures, no wasted retakes. A calm, well-planned setup is a radiation-safety control.

Distance

Step back behind the barrier before the exposure. Dose falls off sharply with distance — the cheapest protection in the room.

Shielding

Gowns, gloves, thyroid shields, and fixed barriers, worn and used correctly by everyone who must remain.

Hands-free first

Never learn “just hold the patient for the picture” as the default. Plan hands-free positioning with sandbags, troughs, foam wedges, tape, and sedation where the veterinarian directs it.

If manual restraint is genuinely unavoidable, it happens under your hospital’s policy: credentialing and supervision rules, full PPE, dosimetry, pregnancy-declaration policy, and never a body part in the primary beam.

Local rules matter: California’s veterinary radiation safety guide excludes people under 18 from performing or assisting with radiographic examinations, and describes personnel monitoring devices including film badges, TLDs, pocket dosimeters, and ring or wrist badges (California Veterinary Medical Board — Radiation Safety Guide (PDF)). Your jurisdiction and your hospital policy set the rules you follow.

Practice

ALARA room sweep

The exposure is thirty seconds away. Check each numbered spot in the room plan below and decide what it is telling you.

ALARA room sweep

Find the radiation-safety failures before the exposure

This is a simplified plan view of a radiography room, drawn for this lesson. Work through the numbered spots in any order — use Tab to move between them and Enter or Space to check one. Each spot is labeled in words and its result is written out in text, so nothing depends on seeing color.

X-ray tableTube headLead barrier & windowDoorShelf

    Check your thinking

    Three ALARA decisions

    One question at a time.

    1. “Step back behind the barrier before the exposure” is mainly which ALARA control?

    2. A teammate suggests holding a paw in the beam so the image is not blurred. What do you do?

    3. Under California’s veterinary radiation safety guide, who must be excluded from performing or assisting with radiographic examinations?

    When a shortcut is suggested, the safe move is always to pause and ask the veterinarian or RVT.

    Sources for this module+
    • CDC — ALARA: As Low As Reasonably Achievable
    • American College of Veterinary Radiology — Radiation Safety Statement
    • California Veterinary Medical Board — Radiation Safety Guide (PDF)

modules.title: Positioning & Restraint Support
modules.completionHeading: Work through the five restraint-plan cases, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
Good positioning support is quiet, planned, and short. It also knows when to stop: patient stability outranks the imaging schedule every single time.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

In this module you will

  • Prepare positioning aids and a restraint plan that keeps hands out of the beam.
  • Protect catheters, oxygen supply, monitoring, and warmth while the patient is positioned.
  • Read stress and distress cues and name them out loud early.
  • Choose the escalation path when a patient’s stability changes mid-study.

Plan the position before you touch the patient

Align, pad, and secure with troughs, sandbags, foam wedges and tape rather than hands. Keep oxygen access and monitoring visible. Keep lines and tubes clear. Label laterality. Agree the pause signal before anyone starts.

Norkus notes that patients in severe cardiac or respiratory distress may need a hands-off, minimalistic approach with oxygen and possible sedation before other procedures, and that in heart failure, stressful diagnostics such as thoracic radiographs may need to wait until the patient is stable (course textbook: Norkus, PDF pp. 45, 124–125; print pp. 29, 108–109).

1

Set the room first

Aids, warmth, non-slip surface, and the study’s views agreed. A patient should not wait on the table while people fetch things.

2

Name the roles

Who positions, who monitors, who is behind the barrier, who calls the stop.

3

Handle gently and briefly

Slow movements, minimal repositioning, quiet voices, and no repeated struggle.

4

Protect the lifelines

Oxygen, IV catheters, monitoring leads, drains and tubes stay accessible and undisturbed.

5

Watch and report

Open-mouth breathing, increased effort, color change, escalating anxiety, or pain: say it immediately.

6

Stop when it stops working

Two failed attempts are a conversation with the veterinarian or RVT, not a third attempt.

Phrases to retire

  • “Just hold harder for one more shot.”
  • “It is only a few seconds, she will be fine.”
  • “We are nearly finished, let us push through.”

Replace them with: “I need to pause — this patient is working harder to breathe. Can you reassess?”

Practice

Choose the restraint plan

Five patients, five decisions. Pick the support action that fits the patient in front of you.

Restraint planning

One patient at a time

Select the best support action, then read the feedback before moving on.

  1. Case 1 of 5

    Stable 4-year-old retriever, left carpus radiograph after a minor fall. Bright, weight-bearing, tolerant of handling.

  2. Case 2 of 5

    Fractious cat, growling and swatting, needs an abdominal series. Physically healthy, no respiratory signs.

  3. Case 3 of 5

    Cat in oxygen, open-mouth breathing when lifted onto the table for thoracic radiographs.

  4. Case 4 of 5

    Dog with a painful abdomen guarding and vocalizing as you attempt a ventrodorsal view.

  5. Case 5 of 5

    Sedated dog being transferred to the CT table. There is an IV catheter, an oxygen line, and a monitor already attached.

The escalation habit: stop, describe what you see, hand the decision to the veterinarian or RVT.

Sources for this module+
  • Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Imaging Service
  • Merck Veterinary Manual — Radiography of Animals
  • Course textbooks (not reproduced here): Norkus, PDF pp. 45, 124–125 (print pp. 29, 108–109) on hands-off handling and delaying stressful thoracic radiographs.

modules.title: Ultrasound Prep & Support
modules.completionHeading: Sort the nine prep tasks and answer the three checks, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
Ultrasound support is mostly preparation: the right patient prep, the right supplies, and a patient who can stay comfortable and still. Interpretation is never part of your role.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

In this module you will

  • Confirm fasting, medication, and bladder instructions before the appointment.
  • Prepare clipping, gel, alcohol, towels, warmth and comfort so the study runs without interruption.
  • Support low-stress positioning, including safer options for a dyspneic patient.
  • Keep language inside scope: describe preparation and patient status, never findings.

Preparation that protects image quality

The University of Minnesota Veterinary Medical Center explains that food and gas can make it harder for ultrasound to penetrate to the organs, and asks clients not to feed pets for twelve hours before an abdominal ultrasound while still allowing water (University of Minnesota Veterinary Medical Center — Ultrasound information for clients). Fasting is exactly the sort of instruction support staff can confirm, document, and flag when it has not been followed.

For focused emergency ultrasound the course textbook is more relaxed about clipping: abdominal point-of-care ultrasound can be performed without clipping, though clipping may improve image quality, minimal restraint is usually enough, and sedation is rarely necessary (course textbook: Blackwell, PDF p. 1620; print p. 1538).

Dyspneic patients change the positioning plan

The course textbook lists dyspneic and trauma patients among the indications for pleural and lung ultrasound, notes that it is focused and does not replace radiographs, full thoracic ultrasound, or physical examination, and recommends avoiding dorsal recumbency in dyspneic or cardiovascularly compromised patients — sternal or standing positions are preferred (course textbook: Blackwell, PDF p. 1623; print p. 1541).

A published case series on lung ultrasound in dogs with pneumothorax similarly describes scanning in sternal, standing, and lateral positions (Frontiers in Veterinary Science — Lung ultrasound in dogs with pneumothorax). Your job is to support whichever position the clinician asks for and to report immediately if the patient stops tolerating it.

Practice

Ultrasound prep sort

Nine tasks are waiting for an abdominal ultrasound appointment. Sort each into the lane that matches what you should actually do with it.

Ultrasound prep sort

Sort every prep task into the right lane

Two steps, one at a time: select a task, then choose the lane it belongs in. Everything is a button, so this works with a keyboard alone. You can move a task again before you check.

Confirm before arrival

Information you verify and document — usually with the owner or the record.

    Prepare in the room

    Physical setup you can complete yourself before the clinician starts.

      Ask the clinician

      Decisions that are outside support scope and need direction.

        Check your thinking

        Two ultrasound decisions

        One question at a time.

        1. Why does fasting matter before an abdominal ultrasound?

        2. The clinician asks for a focused lung scan on a dyspneic dog. Which positioning should you set up for first, if the patient tolerates it?

        3. The scan is running and you notice free fluid on the screen. What is inside your scope?

        Prep is yours. Findings are not.

        Sources for this module+
        • University of Minnesota Veterinary Medical Center — Ultrasound information for clients
        • Frontiers in Veterinary Science — Lung ultrasound in dogs with pneumothorax
        • Merck Veterinary Manual — Overview of Diagnostic Imaging
        • Course textbooks (not reproduced here): Blackwell, PDF pp. 1620–1623 (print pp. 1538–1541) on point-of-care abdominal and lung ultrasound.

modules.title: CT/MRI & Contrast Readiness
modules.completionHeading: Complete both advanced-imaging time-outs, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
CT and MRI are checklist work. Almost everything that goes wrong on an advanced imaging day is something that could have been checked before the patient left the ward.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

In this module you will

  • Run a structured time-out for CT and MRI patients.
  • Screen for ferromagnetic material before anyone approaches the MRI suite.
  • Prepare anesthesia, monitoring, transport, warmth, and recovery support.
  • Complete contrast-readiness checks without ever administering contrast yourself.

Why the checklist exists

MRI is highly sensitive to motion, so small animals generally require general anesthesia, and MRI should be operated by specially trained technologists (Merck Veterinary Manual — MRI in Animals). That means an MRI is never “just a scan”: it is an anesthetic event with airway, monitoring, warmth, and recovery needs attached.

MRI is also sensitive to ferromagnetic material. Merck lists examples that can impair imaging, including microchips, staples, BB or shotgun pellets, stainless-steel sutures, and hemoclips (Merck Veterinary Manual — MRI in Animals). Cornell notes that radiography, ultrasonography, CT and MRI are all in routine veterinary use and that animals may need sedation or anesthesia when movement would defeat the procedure (Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Imaging Service).

Contrast readiness — right patient, right order, right readiness

Support staff prepare for contrast studies; they do not choose or give contrast. Readiness means: the order and route confirmed by the clinician, patient identity verified, IV catheter patent and secured, baseline vital signs recorded, known reaction history flagged, fasting status confirmed, monitoring assigned, and emergency drugs and equipment available per protocol.

A retrospective study of anesthetized dogs and cats evaluated pulse rate, respiratory rate and mean arterial pressure changes after intravenous iohexol for CT and intravenous gadobutrol for MRI (PubMed — Physiologic changes after IV iohexol (CT) and gadobutrol (MRI) in anesthetized dogs and cats). Physiologic change around contrast is the reason monitoring and emergency readiness are part of the checklist.

Unsafe statement to recognize: “give barium if perforation is suspected”. The course textbook specifies an aqueous iodide contrast agent when esophageal perforation is suspected (Blackwell, PDF p. 547; print p. 465). You are not choosing contrast agents — but you should recognize the red flag and speak up.

Practice

Advanced imaging time-out

Two patients are booked. Complete a time-out for each: tick every item that belongs to you, and leave anything that is outside your scope unticked.

Time-out 1 of 2

CT abdomen with intravenous contrast — sedated 8-year-old spaniel

Tick the checks a support team member completes or verifies before this study begins.

A time-out is spoken out loud, with the whole team listening. Silence is not agreement.

Time-out 2 of 2

MRI brain — anesthetized 5-year-old boxer

Same rules. Tick what belongs to support staff for an MRI patient.

If any item cannot be confirmed, the answer is “not yet” — say so before the patient is moved.

Sources for this module+
  • Merck Veterinary Manual — MRI in Animals
  • Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine — Imaging Service
  • PubMed — Physiologic changes after IV iohexol (CT) and gadobutrol (MRI) in anesthetized dogs and cats
  • Course textbooks (not reproduced here): Blackwell, PDF p. 547 (print p. 465) on contrast selection when perforation is suspected; Norkus, PDF pp. 179, 257–258 (print pp. 163, 241–242) on contrast use in obstruction and on advanced imaging in nasal disease.

modules.title: Emergency Imaging Workflow
modules.completionHeading: Work through the three emergency cases and review the credits, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
In an emergency, imaging serves stabilization — not the other way round. Your job is to make the right imaging possible at the right moment, and to protect the patient from the wrong imaging too early.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

In this module you will

  • Apply the rule: stabilize first, use focused bedside imaging when it changes immediate care, defer stressful studies.
  • Prepare bedside ultrasound and radiography support without interrupting resuscitation.
  • Keep oxygen, monitoring, and analgesia in place while imaging happens.
  • Escalate clearly when a patient cannot tolerate the study that has been requested.

The prioritization rule

Stabilize, focus, then image fully

The course textbook places emergency-room ultrasound inside the shock stabilization flow — alongside fluids, laboratory samples, analgesia and antibiotics — and notes that multiple staff members may perform these tasks concurrently (course textbook: Norkus, PDF p. 58; print p. 42). Focused bedside ultrasound is fast, repeatable and comes to the patient, which is why it often precedes a trip to the x-ray room.

The same sources are equally clear about what to delay: stressful diagnostics such as thoracic radiographs may need to wait in fragile heart-failure patients until they are stable (course textbook: Norkus, PDF pp. 124–125; print pp. 108–109), and serial thoracic radiographs are used to monitor response once a patient can tolerate them (course textbook: Blackwell, PDF pp. 1176–1177, 1230; print pp. 1094–1095, 1148).

1

Stabilize and alert

Oxygen, warmth, IV access, analgesia, monitoring. Tell the veterinarian or RVT what you are seeing.

→
2

Bring focused imaging to the patient

Set up bedside ultrasound where it answers the immediate question, without moving an unstable patient.

→
3

Full studies when tolerated

Radiographs and advanced imaging once the clinician judges the patient stable enough. Prepare in advance so it is quick.

Optional clinical image: gas-distended stomach on a radiograph+

Practice

Triage imaging prioritizer

Three emergencies. For each one, choose the next support step, three decisions deep. One decision at a time.

Emergency imaging workflow

Choose the next support step

Each case runs over three decisions. Feedback appears immediately after each choice.

  1. Case A — large-breed dog, retching unproductively, distended abdomen

    The dog has just arrived and the veterinarian is on the way. What do you do first?

    Decision 1 of 3

  2. Case A — large-breed dog, retching unproductively, distended abdomen

    The veterinarian requests a right lateral abdominal radiograph once the dog is supported. What is your best contribution?

    Decision 2 of 3

  3. Case A — large-breed dog, retching unproductively, distended abdomen

    During positioning the dog’s effort to breathe increases sharply. What do you say and do?

    Decision 3 of 3

  4. Case B — cat in oxygen, suspected heart failure, improving but still panicked

    The team is discussing thoracic radiographs. When should they happen?

    Decision 1 of 3

  5. Case B — cat in oxygen, suspected heart failure, improving but still panicked

    The clinician asks for a focused bedside cardiac and lung ultrasound instead. How do you support it?

    Decision 2 of 3

  6. Case B — cat in oxygen, suspected heart failure, improving but still panicked

    The cat tolerates the scan in sternal for ninety seconds, then begins open-mouth breathing. What now?

    Decision 3 of 3

  7. Case C — bitch in prolonged labour, straining without producing a puppy

    The veterinarian is assessing her. What imaging support is most likely to be requested?

    Decision 1 of 3

  8. Case C — bitch in prolonged labour, straining without producing a puppy

    A colleague suggests sedating her so the radiographs are easier to obtain. What is your response?

    Decision 2 of 3

  9. Case C — bitch in prolonged labour, straining without producing a puppy

    How do you prepare so that the study is as short and low-stress as possible?

    Decision 3 of 3

The pattern repeats: stabilize and alert, bring focused imaging to the patient, protect oxygen and monitoring, and defer stressful studies until the patient can tolerate them.

modules.title: Final Assessment

quiz.q: Part 1 · Scenario decisionsA cat arrives in respiratory distress and is placed in oxygen. The team wants thoracic radiographs. As the support team member preparing the room, what is the correct sequence?
opts: Position for radiographs first, then give oxygen if the cat struggles
Continue oxygen and stabilization support, alert the veterinarian, and prepare imaging so it can happen when the cat is judged stable enough
Take one quick view while the cat is still calm from the car journey
Move the cat to the x-ray room and reassess there
quiz.exp: Stabilize first. Stressful diagnostics such as thoracic radiographs may need to wait in fragile patients until the clinician judges them stable enough. Preparing the study in advance is useful; forcing it early is not.

quiz.q: Part 1 · Scenario decisionsMid-way through positioning a dog for an abdominal series, the patient's breathing effort increases noticeably. What do you do?
opts: Finish the current view, then mention it
Reposition into sternal and carry on without interrupting the team
Stop, support the patient, and immediately tell the veterinarian or RVT what has changed
Ask a second person to help hold the dog more firmly
quiz.exp: Stop, support, report. A change in the patient's condition is escalated straight away in plain factual language — the clinician decides what happens to the study.

quiz.q: Part 1 · Scenario decisionsA shocky trauma dog arrives and the clinician asks for focused bedside ultrasound (AFAST/TFAST). What is the support priority?
opts: Move the dog to the ultrasound room where the machine lives
Bring the ultrasound to the patient, continue stabilization support, and prepare monitoring and any sampling supplies requested
Take radiographs first so there is a baseline
Clip the entire abdomen and thorax before the clinician arrives
quiz.exp: Focused bedside imaging exists so that unstable patients do not have to travel. It runs alongside fluids, laboratory samples, analgesia and monitoring, often with several staff working concurrently.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Checklist completenessSelect every item that belongs on a support-staff readiness check before intravenous contrast is given for a CT study.
opts: Patient identity confirmed with two identifiers
Order, contrast agent and route as documented by the clinician
IV catheter patency confirmed and the line secured
Baseline vital signs recorded
Monitoring assigned and emergency drugs and equipment available per protocol
Support staff selecting the contrast dose independently
quiz.exp: Everything except selecting the dose. Physiologic changes have been documented in anesthetized dogs and cats after intravenous iohexol for CT and gadobutrol for MRI, which is why monitoring and emergency readiness are part of readiness. Choosing or changing the contrast plan is never a support-staff task.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Checklist completenessAn MRI brain scan is booked for an anesthetized dog. Select every check that belongs to the support team.
opts: Screen the patient for microchips, staples, pellets, steel sutures and clips
Screen everyone entering the magnet area and remove ferromagnetic items and equipment
Confirm the anesthesia plan and MRI-compatible monitoring with the anesthesia team
Prepare warmth, padding, eye lubrication and a recovery area
Select and run the imaging sequences at the console
quiz.exp: MRI is sensitive to ferromagnetic material — microchips, staples, BB or shotgun pellets, stainless-steel sutures and hemoclips are all listed as materials that can impair imaging. Operating the scanner is the job of specially trained technologists.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Checklist completenessSelect every task a support team member can complete or verify while preparing a patient for an abdominal ultrasound.
opts: Confirm and document fasting status, with water still allowed
Prepare clippers, warmed gel, alcohol and towels
Prepare padding, warmth and a non-slip surface
Decide whether the patient needs sedation for the scan
Tell the owner what the scan is likely to show
quiz.exp: Food and gas can reduce ultrasound penetration, so fasting is a prep instruction you can confirm. Sedation decisions belong to the veterinarian or RVT, and findings are communicated only by the veterinarian.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Radiation safety sweepYou sweep the radiography room ten seconds before an exposure. Select every ALARA failure.
opts: A colleague is standing beside the tube head rather than behind the lead barrier
A helper's hand is at the edge of the collimated field
The room door is standing open
A dosimeter badge is sitting on the shelf instead of being worn
Positioning aids are staged beside the table
quiz.exp: Staged positioning aids are good practice — they are what makes hands-free positioning possible. The other four are failures: distance and shielding, a body part in the primary beam, an uncontrolled door, and unworn personnel monitoring.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Radiation safety sweepWhich single statement best describes the ALARA principle as it applies to your daily work?
opts: Keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable using time, distance and shielding, while still getting a quality study
Take as few radiographs as possible even if the study is incomplete
Radiation risk only applies to the person operating the exposure switch
Lead gloves make it acceptable to hold a patient in the primary beam
quiz.exp: ALARA means as low as reasonably achievable, using the three basic protective measures of time, distance and shielding, while maintaining the quality of the procedure. It never authorizes a body part in the primary beam.

quiz.q: Part 4 · Modality support boundariesMatch the modality to the support task that is most characteristic of it: which pairing is correct?
opts: MRI → confirm fasting and warm the coupling gel
Radiography → screen the patient for microchips and steel sutures
Ultrasound → confirm fasting status, prepare clipping, gel and towels, support low-stress positioning
CT with contrast → decide the contrast agent and dose
quiz.exp: Ultrasound prep is fasting, clipping, gel and comfort. Metal screening belongs to MRI, marker and PPE work belongs to radiography, and contrast selection is never a support-staff decision.

quiz.q: Part 4 · Modality support boundariesWhich pairing of modality and support task is also correct?
opts: Radiography → lead markers, PPE and hands-free positioning aids
Ultrasound → screen every person entering the room for ferromagnetic items
MRI → set kVp and mA for the study
Contrast study → interpret whether the contrast has leaked
quiz.exp: Markers, PPE and positioning aids are core radiography support. Ferromagnetic screening belongs to MRI, technique factors are not a support-staff decision, and interpreting contrast passage or leakage is the veterinarian's role.

quiz.q: Part 5 · Safety red flagsA colleague says: “Esophageal perforation is suspected, so let us get the barium ready.” What should you recognize?
opts: Correct — barium is the standard agent for any esophageal study
Unsafe — an aqueous iodide contrast agent is specified when perforation is suspected; raise it with the veterinarian
It does not matter which agent is used as long as the clinician approves
Barium is fine as long as the volume is small
quiz.exp: When esophageal perforation is suspected, an aqueous iodide contrast agent is used rather than barium. You are not choosing the agent — but recognizing the red flag and raising it is exactly the kind of speaking up this lesson asks for.

quiz.q: Part 5 · Safety red flagsWhich of the following is clearly outside support-staff scope during imaging?
opts: Confirming patient identity, body region and laterality against the order
Reporting that a patient's breathing effort has increased
Describing the lung pattern on a radiograph to the owner
Staging positioning aids and lead markers before the patient arrives
quiz.exp: Interpretation and communication of findings are the veterinarian's role. Support staff prepare, monitor, communicate patient status, and escalate — they do not diagnose.

modules.content:
Twelve questions covering everything in this lesson. One question at a time, immediate feedback, and a pass mark of 80 percent. You can retake it as many times as you need.

Support scope — every module

You do

  • Prepare the patient, room, equipment, and paperwork.
  • Monitor the patient and speak up the moment they change.
  • Communicate what you see in plain, factual language.
  • Escalate to the veterinarian or RVT whenever the plan no longer fits the patient.

You do not

  • Diagnose or interpret any image, or describe findings to an owner.
  • Order, cancel, or change an imaging study on your own.
  • Administer contrast, sedation, or anesthesia.
  • Operate CT, MRI, or fluoroscopy, or set technique beyond your training, credentialing, and direct supervision.

Before you begin

How this assessment works

Questions appear one at a time with a progress indicator. Some questions ask you to select several answers — use the Record response button beneath those. Feedback appears the moment you answer, and you can move back through questions you have already answered.

Your score is shown after the final question. 80% or higher marks this assessment — and the Imaging Support lesson — complete. If you score below that, use Retake assessment and revisit any module from the curriculum first.

What is being tested

Support judgement, not interpretation. Every correct answer is something a support team member prepares, monitors, communicates, or escalates. Nothing in this assessment asks you to read an image or make a clinical decision.
